topic: Weight removed (or added) as the only change: measured effect on quarter-mile time and trap speed or on 0-60, and the drag racer's rule of about a tenth of a second per 100 lb

cases.car: 2025 Ram 1500 (high-end crew-cab trim; engine and transmission not given in the search summaries)
cases.change: About 1,000 lb of sandbags loaded in the bed; nothing else changed (weight ADDED, same truck, same test programme)

physical.ballast: sandbags in the cargo bed, 'about 1,000 lb' (exact weight not given in summary)

cases.measure: Cars.com instrumented drag-strip test: best 0-60 mph and quarter-mile elapsed time and trap speed, bed empty against bed loaded
cases.publisher: Cars.com ('2024 Full-Size Pickup Truck Challenge: Which Truck Is the Fastest?')
cases.note: Summary wording: 'The unloaded run hit a 4.75-second 0-60 time while finishing the quarter-mile in 13 seconds flat at 104.9 mph. Loaded, its best was 5.27 seconds for 0-60 and 13.53 seconds in the quarter-mile at 101.85 mph'; a second summary gives the unloaded trap speed as 104.91 mph and says each truck ran 'empty and with about 1,000 pounds of sandbags in the bed'. Cars.com tested 'the high-end, crew-cab versions of the three trucks' (2024 Ford F-150, 2024 GMC Sierra 1500, 2025 Ram 1500). Arithmetic on the recorded figures: +0.53 s and -3.06 mph in the quarter, +0.52 s to 60 mph, i.e. about 0.053 s of quarter-mile time per 100 lb added. Curb weight, power and engine were not in any summary, so the percentage mass change is unknown from this page alone. 'Before' is the lighter (empty) state and 'after' the heavier (loaded) state. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

cases.car: Ford Crown Victoria Police Interceptor (P71; model year, engine and transmission not given in the search summaries)
cases.change: Car stripped in steps of 300, 600, 800 and finally 1,005 lb removed from a 4,101 lb control weight; only the start and the final step have times in the summaries

physical.weightSteps: 300, 600, 800 and 1,005 lb removed (times for the intermediate steps not in summary)

cases.measure: Eighth-mile drag-strip elapsed time, one run at each weight (video test by TheHoonigans, reported by Jalopnik); trap speed and 0-60 not in any summary
cases.publisher: Jalopnik, reporting a TheHoonigans video ('Here's How Much Quicker A Ford Crown Victoria Gets With 1,000 Pounds Removed')
cases.note: Summary wording: 'They started at a control weight of 4,101 pounds, then dropped weight in steps of 300, 600, 800, and finally 1,005 pounds. The eighth-mile time drops significantly to 10.32 seconds after the 1,005 pounds came out, from the original 10.79.' The article itself warns the test 'isn't particularly scientific, especially with the group apparently only doing one run of each vehicle weight'. This is an EIGHTH-mile time (key eighthMileSec, not one of the README's listed keys), not a quarter-mile time. The final weight is not printed in the summary (4,101 minus 1,005 would be 3,096 lb). Arithmetic on the recorded figures: 0.47 s gained for 1,005 lb, about 0.047 s per 100 lb over the eighth-mile, below the 0.07 s per 100 lb eighth-mile rule quoted under ruleOfThumb. A search summary remarks that 4,101 lb matches a published 2008 Crown Victoria curb weight on a Kelley Blue Book spec page; the car's model year is not stated. An enthusiast video test reported second-hand, not an instrumented magazine test. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

cases.car: Ford Fiesta ST (model year, engine and transmission not given in the search summary)
cases.change: Extreme strip-out including removal of both front and rear doors: 556 lb removed, from 'just over 2,800 lb' to 2,265 lb

physical.removed: 'a lot of parts, including both front and rear doors' (full list not in summary)

cases.measure: 0-62 mph (0-100 km/h) time before and after, owner's video test (Gravel Co) reported by Ford Authority; timing equipment not stated in the summary
cases.publisher: Ford Authority, reporting a Gravel Co video ('Ford Fiesta ST Undergoes Extreme Weight Savings For Speed')
cases.note: Summary wording: the car 'started at just over 2,800 pounds'; after the strip-out 'the car weighed 2,265 pounds, a 556-pound drop. Its 0-62 mph time was 8.38 seconds before the work and 7.29 seconds afterward, 1.09 seconds quicker.' The exact starting weight is not printed (2,265 plus 556 would be 2,821 lb, consistent with 'just over 2,800'). These are 0-62 mph times (key zeroTo62MphSec, not one of the README's listed keys), not 0-60. Arithmetic: about 0.20 s of 0-62 time per 100 lb on a car that lost roughly a fifth of its weight. Caveats: the 2,265 lb figure is with the doors off, so the body's aerodynamics changed as well as its mass, and nothing in the summary says how many runs were made or whether conditions matched. An owner's video test reported second-hand, not an instrumented magazine test. No quarter-mile figure was found for this car. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

cases.car: BMW 330xi (E46; model year, engine and transmission not given in the search summaries)
cases.change: Entire interior removed, each piece weighed, with a stated goal of getting the car under 3,000 lb; weight loss described as about 10% of the original

physical.weightRemoved: about 10% of the original 3,370 lb per one summary; exact pounds removed and final weight not in any summary

cases.measure: 0-60 mph time and 60-0 mph braking distance before and after, owner's video test (ChrisFix) reported by The Drive and others; timing equipment not stated in the summaries
cases.publisher: The Drive, reporting a ChrisFix video ('Here's How Extreme Weight Savings Can Improve Your Car's Performance'); also covered by HotCars and Interesting Engineering
cases.note: Summary wording: 'The car weighed 3,370 lbs and posted a 6.8-second average 0-60 and 60-0 braking distance of 170 ft' (one source lists the 0-60 as 6.77 s); 'He dropped his best 0-60 time to 5.97 seconds and his braking distance to 140ft'; 'The car dropped from a 6.8-second average to 5.97 seconds (a 0.8-second improvement). Its weight loss was about 10% of the original'. The summaries drew on The Drive, HotCars and Interesting Engineering pages without saying which figure came from which. Weak points: (1) the pounds removed are not given exactly, so this case cannot be scored precisely; one summary's 'removing the full interior saves ~200 lbs total' is flagged there as a third-party estimate and conflicts with 'about 10%'; (2) the before figure is an AVERAGE and the after figure a BEST run, so the 0.83 s gain is probably overstated; (3) a 30 ft shorter stop from a roughly 10% weight cut is more than mass alone would normally give on the same tyres, which suggests conditions differed between the two sessions. An owner's video test reported second-hand, not an instrumented magazine test. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

cases.car: Tesla Model 3 Performance (the earlier, pre-2024 version; model year not given in the search summaries)
cases.change: All body panels and exterior lights except the tail lights removed to cut weight; pounds removed NOT given in any summary

physical.removed: 'all panels and exterior lights except the tail lights'

cases.measure: 0-60 mph time, original form against stripped, builders' own video test (B is for Build) reported by InsideEVs; timing equipment not stated in the summaries
cases.publisher: InsideEVs, reporting a B is for Build video ('See How Fast A Tesla Model 3 Without A Body Can Get To 60 MPH'); also Notebookcheck and CarExpert
cases.note: Summary wording: 'the guys at B is for Build managed to accelerate from 0-60 mph in 3.56 seconds with the car still in its original form, while the stripped-down version was over a second faster, reaching 60 mph in 2.46 seconds'. Notebookcheck rounds the same pair to 3.5 s and about 2.5 s. CarExpert says the team ''harvested' all panels and exterior lights except the tail lights in an effort to reduce weight'. NOT SCOREABLE AS IT STANDS: no summary gives the stock or stripped weight, so the size of the change is unknown; the case is kept only because both times are documented, and it needs the weights before the model can be checked against it. Removing the body also changes aerodynamics completely. The stock 3.56 s was measured by the builders on their own car, not a maker's figure (Tesla's claim for the old Model 3 Performance is given in a summary as 3.1 s). A builders' video test reported second-hand, not an instrumented magazine test. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: Removing about 100 lb cuts roughly 0.1 s from a quarter-mile elapsed time (described as the most common rule of thumb in drag racing).
ruleOfThumb.publisher: CNU student capstone paper on drag-racing weight reduction (pcs.cnu.edu)
ruleOfThumb.note: The search summary says the paper 'describes it as the most common rule of thumb in the sport, and it ties to quarter-mile results since most NHRA races run that distance'. A student paper, not a controlled magazine result. Against this page: the three Cars.com pickups lost 0.053, 0.058 and 0.075 s of quarter-mile time per 100 lb of added payload, all below 0.1 s per 100 lb, on heavy trucks whose curb weights were not in the summaries. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: Hot Rod magazine's 'Caddy Hack' (1987), which stripped a 1970 Cadillac Coupe de Ville between passes, averaged 0.095 s of quarter-mile time per 100 lb removed.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: CNU student capstone paper (pcs.cnu.edu), citing Hot Rod magazine second-hand
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary wording: the paper 'reports that 0.095 seconds was reduced per 100 pounds removed from the vehicle on average'; another summary says Hot Rod 'ran a 1970 Cadillac and stripped weight between passes' and 'later ran similar tests, Pontihack and Vette Hack'. A Hagerty article in the results confirms that Hot Rod 'stripped a '70 Coupe De Ville to the bones for its Caddy Hack article' (https://hagerty.com/media/motorsports/heavyweight-hauler-the-flash-cadillac-has-spent-four-plus-decades-flattening-drag-strips/). The original article's baseline weight, final weight and elapsed times were NOT found in three dedicated searches, so Caddy Hack is recorded here as a rule and not as a case. One earlier summary attached 'about 0.07 seconds per 100 pounds' to the Hot Rod test; a later one assigns 0.07 to the eighth-mile, so the 0.095 quarter-mile figure is second-hand and unverified against the magazine. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: On an eighth-mile track the figure is about 0.07 s per 100 lb.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: CNU student capstone paper on drag-racing weight reduction (pcs.cnu.edu)
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'The same paper cites about 0.07 seconds per 100 lb on an 1/8-mile track.' Whether this is the paper's own measured result or a quoted rule is not clear from the summaries. Against this page: the Crown Victoria gained 0.47 s in the eighth for 1,005 lb removed, about 0.047 s per 100 lb. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: 100 lb is worth about 10 rear-wheel horsepower, and each is worth about 0.1 s in the quarter-mile.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: LS1Tech forum, Drag Racing Tech ('Weight vs. horsepower'); the same equivalence appears on The Mustang Source forum
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'The same rule of thumb equates 10 horsepower to about 0.1 second, so 100 lb is roughly 10 rear-wheel horsepower.' Forum lore, not a measurement. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: The tenth-per-100-lb figure is not a constant: it scales with the car's weight-to-power ratio, and lighter cars with less torque are said to gain about 0.1 s for every 55 to 60 lb.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: Honda-Tech forum, drag racing section (other forum posts cited in the note)
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'lighter cars with less torque seem to gain about 0.1 for every 55 to 60 lb' (Honda-Tech); 'One forum post attributes the scaling to the weight-to-power ratio, so the number shifts with the car' (my350z.com); a worked example for a 3,650 lb car trapping 100 mph gives 'about 0.12 seconds per 100 lb, which equals roughly 17.6 feet at that speed' (camaroz28.com, https://www.camaroz28.com/forums/lt1-based-engine-tech-9/true-100lbs-equals-full-car-length-racing-142445/); 'Front-end weight removal may gain more, around 0.12 to 0.15 per 100 lb, according to one owner's experience' (LS1Tech); and 'Wind drag grows with speed and isn't reduced by removing weight, so the benefit shrinks at higher speeds' (Corvette Forum). A separate 2002 forum post says 'removing 20-25 pounds of tires/wheels will net you the same as 100 pounds off the body'. All forum opinion, none measured. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.
